summary: Extends PPP over Ethernet with two optional features: credit-based flow control and a link quality metric report. They help when PPPoE runs over links with changing bandwidth and little buffering, such as mobile point-to-point radio links. It is informational, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: If a water pipe sometimes narrows, you need to know how much can safely flow. This lets one end tell the other how much it can take right now, so nothing overflows.

subtitle: Optional PPPoE extensions that add credit-based flow control and link quality reports for radio links whose bandwidth keeps changing.

tldr.problem: PPPoE works well when both ends have similar, steady bandwidth and buffering. Mobile point-to-point radio links have variable bandwidth and limited buffering, so a fast sender can overrun them.
tldr.mechanism: A peer grants the other side credits, and the other side may only send PPP payload while it holds credits. A separate quality packet (PADQ) reports metrics such as data rate, latency and relative link quality to the router.
tldr.outcome: Both features are optional. The IESG note says the PPP Extensions working group had reservations about the approach and advises implementors to use standard IP routing instead of split termination.

today: RFC 5578 is an Informational, independent-stream RFC that obsoletes RFC 4938, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. The RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: Why PPPoE Needed Extensions
sections.content:
PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) sets up sessions between a Host (the Client) and a traffic-access aggregator (the Server), and carries PPP over real or emulated Ethernet. RFC 5578 observes that it works well when both endpoints have similar bandwidth, forwarding and buffering that do not vary over time.

The target is a radio that sits between two routers. The Radio acts as the PPPoE Client toward its local router (the Server) and talks to a remote Radio over a point-to-point radio link protocol (RLP). Because the radio link changes with mobility, environment and waveform, the Radio can send Link Quality Metrics to the router, which can use them to update route costs. How routing reacts is outside the scope of the RFC.

An IESG note says the PPP Extensions working group had reservations: the feature solves a general problem at an inappropriate layer and may interact unpredictably with other protocols. It advises avoiding split termination and using standard IP routing instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Two walkie-talkies in a field have a signal that gets better and worse. The wire to the radio needs a way to ask how good the signal is right now and how much data it can take.

sections.title: The New TLVs
sections.content:
The extensions add four optional TLVs (type-length-value items, which PPPoE also calls tags). Each starts with a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length, in network byte order.

  • Credits (0x0106) carries two 16-bit numbers: the FCN (Forward Credit Notification), the credits the local node grants to its peer, and the BCN (Backward Credit Notification), the credits remaining at the local node that the peer granted.
  • Metrics (0x0107) reports link quality: resources (a percentage such as remaining battery), relative link quality (0 to 100), a receive-only bit, latency in milliseconds, and the current and maximum data rates with two-bit unit scales (kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s or Tbit/s).
  • Sequence Number (0x0108) is a 16-bit number that pairs a request with its response. It starts at zero and goes up by one for each new request, and a retransmission reuses the old number.
  • Credit Scale Factor (0x0109) sets the size of one credit. The default is 64 bytes and it can range from 1 to 65535 bytes. A value of zero is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: These are four little labelled notes you can stick on a message: how many tickets I give you, how good my signal is, which question this answers, and how big one ticket is.

sections.title: Discovery Stage Packets
sections.content:
The existing PADR (request) and PADS (confirmation) packets may now carry a Credits TLV and a Credit Scale Factor TLV. A Client that wants credit flow control puts a Credits TLV in its PADR, with its initial grant in the FCN and the BCN set to 0. If the Server's PADS includes a Credits TLV back, credit flow control is binding for the whole PPP session stage. The PADS BCN echoes what the Client granted. If the Server does not support credits, it should leave the TLV out, and the Client must terminate a credit-based session the Server cannot support.

The scale factor is fixed during the PADR and PADS exchange and cannot change afterwards. The Client's value applies to credits it grants, and the Server echoes a value for credits it grants.

Three new discovery packets are defined:

  • PADG (code 0x0A) grants more credits at any time after the session starts. It must carry one Credits TLV and one Sequence Number TLV.
  • PADC (code 0x0B) must be sent in answer to a PADG and repeats the PADG's sequence number. Its FCN and BCN show the absolute credits remaining on each side.
  • PADQ (code 0x0C) carries a Metrics TLV to report link metrics. Setting the Metrics TLV length to zero turns it into a query.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the game starts, each side says whether it wants to use tickets. If both agree, they must keep to it. During the game they can hand out more tickets and ask each other how the signal is.

sections.title: How Credits Control the Flow
sections.content:
Credit accounting applies only to packets sent in the PPP session stage. Once credit flow is agreed, a node must be granted credits before its peer is allowed to send it payload. Each node keeps two running counters: credits a peer has granted to it, which drop with every packet it sends, and credits it has granted, which drop with every packet it receives. When its own counter reaches zero, a node must stop transmitting. Packets that arrive after the granted credits are used up are discarded.

Credits are counted in the session's scale unit and rounding is always up. With the default 64-byte unit, 128 bytes of PPP payload uses 2 credits and 130 bytes uses 3. A grant is an increment from 1 to 0xffff, and a value of zero is a NULL grant. Once credits have been granted, they must be honored.

Grants can be out-of-band (PADG and PADC in the discovery stage) or in-band, with a Credits TLV placed at the start of a PPP session packet. In-band grants are not acknowledged but show up in the peer's own in-band traffic, which is the most efficient option when traffic is heavy.

If a PADC does not come back in time, the sender should send a new PADG with zero credits, the same sequence number and a doubled wait. Because packets in transit can make the two sides disagree, the BCN fields can be used to reset the peer's credit values after larger errors.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a bus that only lets passengers on when the driver hands out tickets. When you run out of tickets you wait for more, and the driver can give you extra tickets whenever there is room.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The memo adds flow control on top of the existing PPPoE security mechanisms from RFC 2516 and does not add new ones. It does require that the Service TLV and the Session ID always be validated before credits are processed. A Credits TLV sent outside an established credit-based session must be ignored.

IANA assigned the four TLV values (262 to 265, that is 0x0106 to 0x0109) and the three PPPoE codes 10, 11 and 12 (0x0a, 0x0b, 0x0c) to this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you accept a ticket, check that it came from the right person for the right trip.

messages.note: Reports the remaining credits on each side.
